x: Commentary on Sūrat al-Muddaththir. In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “O you who are cloaked! Rise and warn. Magnify your Lord. Purify your garments. Shun defilement. Do not give in order to receive more. For your Lord, be patient” (74:1–7).

By “O you who are cloaked,” exalted is His praise, He means: O you wrapped in your clothes while sleeping. It is related that God’s Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was addressed this way while wrapped in a cloak.
Among those who said this:

c: Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā related to us from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd, from Shuʿbah, from al-Mughīrah, from Ibrāhīm,
m: regarding “O you who are cloaked”: “He was wrapped in a cloak.” It is related that this was the first thing revealed from the Qur’an to God’s Messenger, and that he was told, “O you who are cloaked.”

c: Yūnus ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us from Ibn Wahb, from Yūnus, from Ibn Shihāb, from Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, that Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī said:
m: The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, spoke about the pause in revelation: “As I was walking, I heard a voice from the sky. I raised my head, and there was the angel who had come to me at Ḥirāʾ, seated on a throne between heaven and earth.” The Messenger of God said: “I was terrified by him, so I returned and said, ‘Wrap me up, wrap me up!’ They covered me, and God, mighty and exalted, revealed: ‘O you who are cloaked! Rise and warn. Magnify your Lord,’ through ‘Shun defilement.’” He said: “Then revelation came in succession.”
b.via: that Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Anṣārī

c: Ibn al-Muthannā related to us from al-Walīd ibn Muslim, from al-Awzāʿī, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, who said:
m: I asked Abū Salamah, “Which part of the Qur’an was revealed first?” He said, “‘O you who are cloaked.’” Another report from Yaḥyā gives the same answer. I said, “People say, ‘Recite in the name of your Lord’

.” Abū Salamah said: I asked Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh which part of the Qur’an was first revealed, and he said, “‘O you who are cloaked.’” I said, “People say, ‘Recite in the name of your Lord who created.’” He said: “I will tell you only what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, told us. He said, ‘I was staying at Ḥirāʾ. When I finished my retreat, I descended and went down into the valley. I was called, so I looked to my right, my left, behind me, and in front of me, but saw nothing.’ He continued: ‘Then I looked above my head and saw him seated on a throne between heaven and earth. I was terrified’”—as ʿUthmān ibn ʿUmar related it; the wording is, “I was overcome with terror”—“and went to Khadījah. I said, ‘Cover me!’ They covered me and poured water over me. Then God revealed to me, ‘O you who are cloaked! Rise and warn.’”

c: Abū Kurayb related to us from Wakīʿ, from ʿAlī ibn al-Mubārak, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr, who said:
m: I asked Abū Salamah about the first revelation from the Qur’an. He said, “‘O you who are cloaked’ was revealed first.” I said, “They say it was ‘Recite in the name of your Lord who created.’” He replied: “I asked Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, and he said, ‘I will relate only what the Messenger of God told us. He said: I passed by Ḥirāʾ, and when I finished my retreat and descended, I heard a voice. I looked to my right and saw nothing; to my left and saw nothing; in front of me and saw nothing; behind me and saw nothing. Then I raised my head and saw something. I went to Khadījah and said, “Cover me, and pour water over me!” They covered me and poured cold water over me, and “O you who are cloaked” was revealed.’”

c: Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related to us from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhrī, who said:
m: Revelation paused for a time for the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, and he became deeply distressed. He would go to the high peaks of the mountains, intending to throw himself down. Whenever he reached a summit, Gabriel, peace be upon him, would appear to him and say, “You are God’s Prophet,” calming his heart and restoring his spirit. The Prophet used to speak about this and said: “One day, as I was walking, I saw the angel who used to come to me at Ḥirāʾ seated on a throne between heaven and earth. I was terrified and returned to Khadījah, saying, ‘Wrap me up!’ They wrapped me up”—that is, covered me—“and God revealed: ‘O you who are cloaked! Rise and warn. Magnify your Lord. Purify your garments.’” Al-Zuhrī said: The first thing revealed to him was “Recite in the name of your Lord who created,” through “what he did not know”

x: The interpreters differed over “O you who are cloaked.”
Some said it means, “O you who are sleeping in your clothes.”
Those who said this include: Ibn ʿAbbās said, “O you who are sleeping.” Qatādah explained it as “the one wrapped in his clothes.”
Others said it means: O you who are cloaked with prophethood and its burdens.
Those who said this include: Dāwūd was asked about the verse and related from ʿIkrimah that he said: “You have been entrusted with this affair, so rise and carry it out.”

Regarding “Rise and warn”: God Most High says to His Prophet Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him: Rise from your sleep and warn your people who associate partners with God and worship other than Him of God’s punishment.
The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah explained it as warning of God’s punishment, the calamities that befell earlier peoples, and the severity of His vengeance.
Regarding “Magnify your Lord”: God Most High says: Muḥammad, magnify your Lord by worshiping Him and directing your hopes and needs to Him, not to any other deity or rival.
Regarding “Purify your garments”: the interpreters differed.

Some said it means: do not wear your clothes in disobedience or treachery. Ibn ʿAbbās cited Ghaylān ibn Salamah’s verse: “Praise be to God, I have worn no garment of a sinner, nor covered myself with treachery.” Abū Kurayb related that a man came to Ibn ʿAbbās while I was sitting there and asked about the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās said: “Do not wear them in disobedience or treachery.” He then cited Ghaylān’s verse. ʿIkrimah said it means do not wear them in treachery or sin, and recited the same verse. Ibn Ḥumayd related from Mihrān, from Sufyān, from al-Ajlaḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Kindī, from ʿIkrimah, that “Purify your garments” means do not wear them in disobedience. He cited Ghaylān’s line: “Praise be to God, I have worn no garment of a sinner, nor covered myself with treachery.” Ibn ʿAbbās said “purify your garments” means from sin; in Arabic, someone with clean garments is described as pure. Another report from him gives the same explanation.

Ibrāhīm said it means cleanse them of sins. Ibn ʿAbbās likewise said: “From sins.” Ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿlā related from Ibn Thawr, from Maʿmar, from Qatādah, regarding “Purify your garments”: he said this is an Arabic expression; they would say “purify your garments,” meaning from sin. Qatādah also said to cleanse them of disobedience: Arabs called a man who broke his word “filthy in his clothes,” and when he kept his word and acted rightly they said he was “pure in his clothes.” Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibrāhīm explained it as cleansing from sin. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Do not wear your clothes while disobeying God. Ibn ʿAbbās likewise said: “From sin.” Ibrāhīm said: “From sin.” ʿIkrimah said: “Do not wear your clothes in disobedience.” ʿĀmir and ʿAṭāʾ said: “From sins.”

Others said it means do not wear clothes obtained through impure earnings. Ibn ʿAbbās said: “Do not let the clothes you wear come from unlawful earnings”; it is also said to mean do not wear clothes in disobedience.

Others said it means: Put your deeds right. Mujāhid said: “Your deeds—set them right.” Abū Razīn explained it as setting one’s deeds right. Arabs would call someone with evil deeds “filthy in his clothes,” and someone whose deeds were good “pure in his clothes.”
Others, reporting from Mujāhid, said: “You are neither a soothsayer nor a sorcerer, so turn away from what they say.”

Others said it means: wash your clothes with water and purify them of filth. Ibn Sīrīn said: “Wash them with water.” Ibn Zayd said the polytheists did not purify themselves, so God commanded His Prophet to purify himself and his clothes. The interpretation given by Ibn Sīrīn and Ibn Zayd—that he should wash his clothes—is the most apparent meaning. The view of Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrimah, and most early authorities is that “your garments” refers to your person: purify yourself of sins. God knows best what He intended. Regarding “Shun defilement”: the reciters differed. Some Medinese reciters and most Kufans read al-rijz with kasrah on the rāʾ; some Meccan and Medinese reciters read al-rujz with ḍammah. Those who read it with ḍammah understood it as idols, so the meaning is: leave the worship and service of idols. Those who read it with kasrah understood it as punishment: shun the deeds that bring punishment upon you.

In our view both are established readings, and either is correct; the two vowels are dialectal variants with the same meaning. We have not found early interpreters distinguishing between the meanings; as far as we know, al-Kisāʾī was the first to distinguish them.
The interpreters differed over the meaning here.
Some said it means idols. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as wrath, meaning idols.

x: Mujāhid said it means idols. Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah likewise said “idols.” Qatādah said it means Isāf and Nāʾilah, two idols near the House whose faces were touched by those who passed by them; God commanded His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to avoid and keep away from them. Al-Zuhrī said it means idols. Ibn Zayd said it means the deities they worshiped; God commanded him to abandon them, neither visit nor approach them.

Others said it means: shun disobedience and sin. Ibrāhīm said it means sin. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: Shun disobedience. We have already explained the meaning of rijz, with supporting evidence, so there is no need to repeat it here. Regarding “Do not give in order to receive more”: the interpreters differed.

Some said it means: Muḥammad, do not give a gift hoping to receive something greater in return. Ibn ʿAbbās said: “Do not give a gift seeking something better than it.” Ḍamrah ibn Ḥabīb and Abū al-Aḥwaṣ said: “Do not give something in order to receive more than it.”

ʿIkrimah said the same: do not give something in order to receive more. He also said: do not give a gift intending to take back more. Ibrāhīm said: “Do not give in order to increase your return.” Another report from him gives the same explanation. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise said not to give in order to receive more. Another report says: do not give something to take back more. Ibrāhīm said: do not give something to increase your return. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said this refers to a permissible form of usury that was specific to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. He also said there are two kinds of usury, permitted and forbidden: permitted usury is gifts, and forbidden usury is interest. Qatādah said: Do not give anything seeking the compensation and return of this world. Another report from Qatādah says: Do not give anything seeking to be repaid with something better. Ṭāwūs said the same. Mujāhid said: Do not give wealth as a favor, hoping for a better reward in this world.

Ibrāhīm said: Do not give in order to receive more. Ibrāhīm also said: Do not give in order to increase your return. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said this command was specifically for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, while people generally have latitude in this matter.

Others said it means: Do not consider your deeds a favor to your Lord or regard them as abundant. Al-Ḥasan said: Do not regard your deeds as abundant before your Lord. He said similarly in another report. He also said: Do not count your deeds as many. Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: Do not let your deeds seem great in your own eyes, for they are small compared with what God has bestowed and given you.

Others said it means: Do not grow weak in doing good, lest you do too much of it. They understood tamnun as “grow weak,” from the phrase “a manīn rope,” meaning a weak rope. Mujāhid said: Do not grow weak in doing more good; in Arabic, tamunn means “you grow weak.”

Others said: Do not hold your prophethood over people as a favor and seek payment from them for it. Ibn Zayd said: Do not hold the prophethood and Qur’an with which We sent you over them to gain compensation from worldly life. In our view, the soundest interpretation is: Do not regard your good deeds as abundant in relation to your Lord. We consider this preferable because the surrounding verses command God’s Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to strive in calling people to Him and to be patient with the harm he encounters for His sake. This interpretation fits that context better than the others. It is related that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd recited it as “Do not give in order to receive more.” Regarding “For your Lord, be patient”: God Most High says: For your Lord, be patient through the hardships you encounter for His sake.

The interpreters expressed this in different ways. Mujāhid said: “Be patient with the harm you suffer.” Ibn Zayd said: “He was charged with a tremendous task: fighting the Arabs for God, then the non-Arabs after the Arabs.”

evidence.text: It is related that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd recited it as “Do not give in order to receive more.”

x: Others said it means: Be patient in giving what you give. Ibrāhīm said: “Be patient with your gift.” Another report says: “Be patient with what you give for God.” Ibrāhīm also said: “Be patient in giving it.”
Others said it means: Be patient for your Lord in what you give. Ibrāhīm said: “Be patient in giving.” Another report from him says: “Be patient in what you give for God.”

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “When the trumpet is blown, that will be a difficult day, not easy for the disbelievers. Leave Me to deal with the one I created alone and gave abundant wealth” (74:8–12).
“When the trumpet is blown” means when the horn is blown. “That will be a difficult day” means a hard day.

The interpreters said similarly. Ibn ʿAbbās related that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: “How can I be at ease when the one who blows the horn has placed it to his mouth, lowered his forehead, and is listening for when he will be commanded to blow?” The Companions asked, “What should we say?” He replied, “Say: God is sufficient for us, and He is the best trustee; in God we place our trust.” Ikrimah said “when the trumpet is blown” means when the horn is blown. Mujāhid said the same, explaining that it is like a horn. Ibn ʿAbbās said it is the day the trumpet is blown, and the nāqūr is what is blown. Ibn ʿAbbās also related that the Prophet went out to his Companions and said: “How can I be at ease when the one who blows the horn has placed it to his mouth, lowered his forehead, and turned his ear to listen for when he will be commanded to sound the blast?” This troubled his Companions, so he instructed them to say: “God is sufficient for us, and He is the best trustee; in God we place our trust.”

Ibn ʿAbbās explained the nāqūr as the trumpet and the day as difficult. Al-Ḥasan said it means when the trumpet is blown. Qatādah said the nāqūr is the trumpet, and al-ṣūr refers to creation; “that will be a difficult day” means a hard day. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas also explained it as the trumpet. Ibn Zayd said it means the trumpet.

Regarding “Leave Me to deal with the one I created alone”: God Most High says to His Prophet Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him: Entrust to Me the affair of the one I created alone in his mother’s womb, with no wealth or children. It is said that this refers to al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah al-Makhzūmī. Ibn ʿAbbās reported that God revealed “Leave Me to deal with the one I created alone” about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, as well as
“By your Lord, We will surely question them all”

and what follows. Mujāhid explained it as: I created him alone, with neither wealth nor children. Another report from Mujāhid says it was revealed about al-Walīd, as is the case for all creation. Qatādah said this was al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, whom God brought forth from his mother’s womb alone, with no wealth or children, then gave wealth, children, and abundant increase. Ibn Zayd said these verses, through “This is nothing but transmitted magic” and “I will cast him into Saqar,” were revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk likewise said “the one I created alone” means al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah.
Regarding “and gave him abundant wealth”: the interpreters differed over what this wealth was and how much it amounted to.
Some said it was dinars totaling one thousand. Mujāhid said his wealth was one thousand dinars. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also said one thousand dinars.
Others said it was four thousand dinars. Sufyān said he had heard it was four thousand dinars.
Others said the wealth was land. Al-Nuʿmān ibn Sālim said it was land, as did another report from him.

Others said it was a month-by-month income. ʿUmar reportedly said “abundant wealth” meant income accruing each month. Abū Ḥafṣ al-Jubayrī related from Ḥalbas al-Ḍubaʿī, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAṭāʾ, the same explanation, without attributing it to ʿUmar. Another report through Ḥalbas gives the same. A report from Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh also gives it from ʿAṭāʾ, from ʿUmar. The soundest thing to say is what God said: “I gave him abundant wealth”—a large amount, whether abundant in number or extent.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “And sons present with him; I made things easy for him. Yet he hopes that I will give him more. No indeed! He has been obstinate toward Our signs. I will burden him with an arduous ascent” (74:13–17).
God means, “I gave him sons present with him.” It is reported they were ten. Mujāhid said they were ten sons.

Regarding “I made things easy for him”: God Most High says He expanded his life and made it comfortable. Sufyān said he was given abundance. Mujāhid explained it as wealth and children. Regarding “Yet he hopes that I will give him more”: He hopes and expects that I will give him more wealth and children beyond what I have already given him. “No indeed” means he will not receive the worldly wealth, children, and ease he hopes for. “He has been obstinate toward Our signs” means that this man whom I created alone has opposed Our signs—the proofs God has sent to His creation through scriptures and messengers—and turned away from the truth like a stubborn camel.
“When you descend, put me in the middle, for I am old and cannot endure the stubborn ones.”

Ibn ʿAbbās said he was a denier of God’s signs. Mujāhid said he opposed them and turned away from them; another report says he was opposed to the truth and distant from it. Qatādah said he was ungrateful for and denied God’s signs. Sufyān said he was hostile and opposed.

Mujāhid explained ʿanīdan as opposing the truth and turning away from it. Qatādah said he was ungrateful and denied God’s signs. Sufyān said it means hostile and contentious; ʿanīd is one who opposes, like “a coming year,” which means the year that follows. Regarding “I will burden him with an arduous ascent”: God Most High says: I will impose upon him a painful punishment with no relief. It is said that al-Ṣaʿūd is a mountain of fire that the people of Hell will be forced to climb. Those who transmitted this include: Muḥammad ibn ʿUmārah al-Asadī related from Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd ibn Zāʾidah, who said: Sharīk related from…

ʿAmmār al-Duhnī, from ʿAṭiyyah, from Abū Saʿīd, from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, regarding “I will burden him with an arduous ascent.” He said: “It is a mountain of fire in Hell that they will be made to climb. When he places his hand on it, it melts; when he lifts it, it returns, and the same happens when he places his foot.” ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith related from Darraj, from Abū al-Haytham, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, from the Messenger of God, who said: “Al-Ṣaʿūd is a mountain of fire. He climbs it for seventy years, then is hurled down it for the same length of time, forever.” Mujāhid explained it as an arduous punishment. Qatādah said it is a punishment with no relief. Another report from Qatādah says it is a punishment with no rest. (The commentary continues.) Mujāhid said al-ṣaʿūd is hardship in punishment. Ibn Zayd said it is toil from punishment.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “He thought and devised. So may he be destroyed—how he devised! Again, may he be destroyed—how he devised! Then he looked, then he frowned and scowled, then he turned away and acted arrogantly, saying: ‘This is nothing but transmitted magic. This is nothing but the speech of human beings’” (74:18–25).

God Most High says that the man I created alone thought about the Qur’an God sent down to His servant Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and calculated what he would say about it. “May he be destroyed—how he devised!” means: May he be cursed for what he devised to say about it. “Again, may he be destroyed—how he devised!” means: Then may he be cursed for how he devised his statement about it. “Then he looked” means he deliberated. “Then he frowned” means he knitted his brow, “and scowled,” meaning he grimaced and showed displeasure. Tawbah ibn al-Ḥumayr said: “Her turning away troubled me, as did her refusal of my request and her scowling.” Reports describe the one who did this. Among those who reported this: ʿIkrimah said that al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah came to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who recited the Qur’an to him. He seemed moved by it. When Abū Jahl heard, he went to him and said, “Uncle, your people want to gather money for you.”

He asked why. Abū Jahl said, “They would give it to you because you went to Muḥammad, seeking what he has.” Al-Walīd replied, “Quraysh knows I have the most wealth among them.” Abū Jahl said, “Then say something about him so your people know you reject and dislike what he says.” Al-Walīd asked what to say, adding: “By God, there is no man among you more knowledgeable than I about poetry, its rajaz, its odes, or the poetry of the jinn. By God, what he says resembles none of this. His words have sweetness; they shatter what is beneath them and rise above, with nothing rising above them.” Abū Jahl said, “Your people will not be satisfied until you say something against him.” Al-Walīd said, “Let me think.” Then he said: “This is magic transmitted from another.” Thus “Leave Me to deal with the one I created alone” was revealed. Qatādah said al-Walīd came from his mother’s womb alone, and the verses were revealed about him through “over it are nineteen.”

Ibn ʿAbbās said al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah visited Abū Bakr ibn Abī Quḥāfah to ask about the Qur’an. After Abū Bakr explained it, al-Walīd went out to Quraysh and said: “How astonishing is what Ibn Abī Kabshah says! By God, it is neither poetry, nor magic, nor the rambling of madness. His words are from God.” When a group of Quraysh heard this, they conspired, saying: “If al-Walīd converts, all Quraysh will convert.” Abū Jahl said, “I will handle him.” He went to al-Walīd and said, “Have you seen your people gathering charity for you?” Al-Walīd replied, “Am I not the wealthiest and most blessed with children among them?” Abū Jahl said: “They say you visit Ibn Abī Quḥāfah only to get some of his food.” Al-Walīd said that his clan had said this. “By the oath of Jābir ibn Quṣayy, I will not go near Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or Ibn Abī Kabshah. His words are only transmitted magic.” God then revealed to His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, “Leave Me to deal with the one I created alone,” through “it leaves nothing and spares nothing.”

Qatādah related al-Walīd’s reflection: “By God, I considered what this man says. It is not poetry, but it has sweetness and beauty; it rises above and nothing rises above it. I have no doubt it is magic.” God revealed “So may he be destroyed—how he devised!” and “then he frowned and scowled”—he knitted his brow and grimaced. Mujāhid said al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah thought and devised at the council house. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said these verses refer to al-Walīd, whom the Prophet invited to Islam. He said, “Let me consider it,” then thought, looked, frowned and scowled, turned away and acted arrogantly, and said, “This is nothing but transmitted magic.” God assigned him Saqar. Ibn Zayd said al-Walīd told his people, “Tonight I will examine this man for you.” He went to the Prophet and found him standing in prayer, reciting. When his people asked what he thought, al-Walīd said, “I heard sweet, fresh, fruitful words that capture hearts.”

They said, “It is poetry.” He replied, “No, by God, it is not poetry. No one knows poetry better than I. Have not the poets, al-Nābighah and others, recited their poetry to me?” They said, “Then he is a soothsayer.” Al-Walīd said, “No, by God, he is not a soothsayer; I know soothsaying.” They said, “Then it is the magic of the ancients that he has written down.” He said, “I do not know. If it is something, then perhaps it is transmitted magic.”
“So may he be destroyed—how he devised!
Again, may he be destroyed—how he devised!” He said: he was destroyed in his devising when he said it was not poetry, then again when he said it was not soothsaying.

Regarding “Then he turned away and acted arrogantly”: He turned away from believing in and affirming what God revealed of His Book, and acted arrogantly toward acknowledging the truth. He said, “This is nothing but transmitted magic”—the Qur’an Muḥammad recites is only magic that he has taken from someone else.
The interpreters said similarly. Abū Razīn explained “transmitted magic” as “he takes it from another.” Another report from Abū Razīn says: “He transmits it from another.”

Regarding “This is nothing but the speech of human beings”: God Most High reports the individual’s claim about the Qur’an: “What Muḥammad recites is nothing but the speech of human beings”—that is, the words of a son of Adam, not the speech of God.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “I will cast him into Saqar. What will make you know what Saqar is? It leaves nothing and spares nothing. It scorches the skin. Over it are nineteen. We have appointed only angels as keepers of the Fire, and We have made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve, so that those given the Scripture may be certain, the believers may increase in faith, and those given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt; and so that those in whose hearts is sickness and the disbelievers may say, ‘What did God mean by this example?’ Thus God leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills. None knows the forces of your Lord except Him. This is only a reminder to humanity” (74:26–31).
“I will cast him into Saqar” means I will bring him to one of the gates of Hell, named Saqar. It is not declined because Saqar is one of the names of Hell.

Regarding “What will make you know what Saqar is?” God Most High says: What, Muḥammad, could make you know what Saqar is? Then He, mighty and exalted, explained it: it is a fire that “leaves nothing”—leaves no one alive—“and spares nothing,” leaving no one dead, but burns them whenever their creation is renewed.

The interpreters said similarly. Mujāhid said “it leaves nothing and spares nothing” means it neither kills nor lets live. Another report from Mujāhid gives the same. Mazīdah said it consumes them completely, and whenever they are recreated for it, it does not spare them but takes and consumes them.

Regarding “It scorches the skin”: God Most High means it changes the skin of those in it. Lawwāḥah is an adjective describing Saqar, raised in the nominative to agree with it. Though lawwāḥah is indefinite and Saqar definite, the nominative is sound because the adjective conveys praise. Mujāhid explained “It scorches the skin” as the skin. Abū Razīn said it gives the skin a blast, leaving it darker than night. Zayd ibn Aslam said their bodies are scorched in it. Qatādah said it burns the skin. Ibn ʿAbbās said it burns human skin. Ibn Zayd said it changes and burns the skin; one says a person is scorched by exposure to the sky, and the Fire changes their colors. Abū Razīn said it changes their skin and makes it black. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said it burns human skin. A report from Ibn ʿAbbās says muʿarriḍah. I suspect this report from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah from Ibn ʿAbbās is mistaken, and that the word should be mughayyirah (“changing”), but has been miscopied.

Regarding “Over it are nineteen”: God Most High says there are nineteen keepers over Saqar. It is related that when this was revealed to the Messenger of God, Abū Jahl said—as Ibn ʿAbbās reported—when he heard “Over it are nineteen” through “the believers may increase in faith”: “May your mothers lose you! I hear Ibn Abī Kabshah telling you that the keepers of the Fire are nineteen, while you are the strongest multitude. Can’t every ten of you overpower one of Hell’s keepers?” God then revealed to His Messenger to go to Abū Jahl, take him by the hand in the valley of Mecca, and say to him,
“Woe to you, and again woe! Again woe to you, and again woe!”

When the Messenger of God did this, Abū Jahl said, “By God, neither you nor your Lord can do anything.” God disgraced him at Badr. Qatādah said Abū Jahl remarked: “Can’t every ten of you overcome one keeper of the Fire, when you are the strongest multitude? Your companion tells you that there are nineteen over it.” Another report from Qatādah gives the same statement. Ibn Zayd said there are nineteen keepers of Saqar.

Regarding “We have appointed only angels as keepers of the Fire”: God Most High says He appointed only angels as keepers of the Fire. This answers Abū Jahl’s question to Quraysh, “Can’t every ten of you overpower one of them?” Who can overpower the keepers of the Fire when they are angels? Ibn Zayd said: God did not make them men, so that each man could seize one of them, as Abū Jahl claimed.

Regarding “We have made their number only a trial for those who disbelieve”: We made the number of these keepers a trial for the Quraysh polytheists who disbelieve in God. Qatādah explained it as a trial. God made the report about the number of Hell’s keepers a trial for the disbelievers because they denied it and one of them said to his companions, “I alone can handle them.” Mujāhid said the nineteen were made a trial. Abū al-Ashadd ibn al-Jumaḥī said: “They will not reach my ankles before I drive them away from Hell.”

Regarding “so that those given the Scripture may be certain”: God Most High means that the people of the Torah and Gospel may be certain of the truth of what their books report about the number of Hell’s keepers when it agrees with what God, mighty and exalted, revealed in His Book to Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him. Ibn ʿAbbās said the Torah and Gospel state that they are nineteen; God intended the People of the Book to become certain and the believers to increase in faith. Mujāhid said they find the number of the keepers of the Fire written in their scriptures. Qatādah said the Qur’an confirms the earlier books—the Torah and Gospel—which all state that the keepers of the Fire are nineteen. Another report from Qatādah says that the People of the Book become certain when the number of the keepers of the Fire agrees with what is in their books. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the Torah and Gospel give the number of Hell’s keepers as nineteen. Ibn Zayd said it means that they may become certain that you are God’s Messenger.

Regarding “and the believers may increase in faith”: God Most High says that those who believe in God will increase in their affirmation of God and His Messenger by affirming the number of the keepers of Hell. Regarding “and those given the Scripture and the believers may not doubt”: the people of the Torah and Gospel will not doubt the truth of this, nor will the believers in God from the community of Muḥammad, peace and blessings be upon him.

Regarding “and so that those in whose hearts is sickness and the disbelievers may say”: God Most High means the hypocrites, whose hearts are sick, and the Quraysh polytheists who disbelieve in God. They say, “What did God mean by this example?” Qatādah explained “sickness in their hearts” as hypocrisy. Ibn Zayd said they were asking this because God frightens them by mentioning the nineteen.

Regarding “Thus God leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills”: Just as God led astray these hypocrites and polytheists who asked what God intended by mentioning the number of Hell’s keepers, He guided the believers through it, so that their faith increased as they affirmed it. “Thus God leaves astray whom He wills” among His creation, abandoning them so they fail to reach the truth, “and guides whom He wills,” granting them success in reaching what is correct. “None knows the forces of your Lord” in their number except Him—God.

Qatādah said “None knows the forces of your Lord except Him” means no one knows their great number except Him. Regarding “This is only a reminder to humanity”: God Most High says the Fire He has described is only a reminder by which He admonishes human beings, the children of Adam.
The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah and Mujāhid explained it as the Fire.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “No indeed! By the moon, by the night as it withdraws, and by the dawn as it brightens: it is indeed one of the greatest things, a warning to humanity—to whoever among you wishes to advance or fall behind” (74:32–37).

“No indeed” means that the claim of the one who said he could handle the nineteen keepers of Hell for his polytheist companions is false. Then our Lord, exalted is His praise, swore: “By the moon, and by the night as it withdraws”—
that is, as the night departs.

The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said it means when the night passes. Ibn ʿAbbās said that the night’s withdrawal is its darkening. The reciters differed: most Medinese and Basran reciters, along with some Meccan and Kufan reciters, read “idh adbara” (“when it departs”). Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ reportedly said Quraysh say “the night departed.” Some Meccan, Medinese, and Kufan reciters read “idhā dabara” (“when it has passed”). In our view both are established readings with sound meanings, and whichever one is recited is correct. A reciter who reads either way is correct. Scholars of Arabic differed. Some Kufans said both are dialects: one says dabara al-nahār or adbara al-nahār (“the day departed”), and dabara al-ṣayf or adbara al-ṣayf (“summer passed”), just as qabala and aqbala are used. But when they say “the rider came” or “departed,” they use the alif. Some Basrans said “by the night when it has passed” means when the night comes after the day and reaches its end. One says dabaranī when something comes behind me, and adbara when it turns away. In my view both are dialectal forms with the same meaning. Arabs say, “May God disgrace what came before and what came after.” Moreover, the interpreters did not distinguish between the two readings, which shows that they understood them as synonymous.

Some Meccan, Medinese, and Kufan reciters read “idhā dabara” (“when it has passed”).

x: Regarding “and by the dawn as it brightens”: God Most High says, “By the dawn when it shines.” Qatādah said it means when the dawn brightens and arrives. “It is indeed one of the greatest things” means that Hell is one of the great and tremendous matters. Mujāhid, Qatādah, Abū Razīn, Ibn Zayd, and others said it means Hell. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said it means Hell. Ibn ʿAbbās likewise explained it as Hell.
Regarding “a warning to humanity”: God Most High says Hell is one of the greatest matters, a warning to the children of Adam.
The interpreters differed about what is described as “a warning to humanity.”

Some said it refers to Hell and is an adjective of the pronoun in “it is indeed,” with “warning” in the accusative as a detached description after “one of the greatest things,” a definite phrase. Qatādah related from al-Ḥasan: “By God, people have not been warned of anything more dreadful, nor of any calamity more dreadful than it.”

Others said “a warning” describes God Most High, a report from Him about Himself: He is a warner to His creation. On this interpretation, “a warning” is outside the preceding sentence, meaning: We appointed no keepers of the Fire except angels, as a warning to humanity—that is, as an admonition. It is like
“You will know what My warning is”

meaning “My admonition.” It can also mean: We made Hell one of the greatest things as a warning. This is the intended meaning of those who hold this view, God willing. Abū Razīn said: “It is Hell, and God says: I am a warner to you about it, so beware of it.”

Others said it describes the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, with “a warning” in the circumstantial accusative from “rise”: rise as a warner to humanity and warn them. Ibn Zayd said “humanity” means the people, the children of Adam; when asked whether Muḥammad is the warner, he replied, “Yes, he warns them.”

Regarding “to whoever among you wishes to advance or fall behind”: God Most High says Hell is a warning to humanity, to whoever among you wishes to advance in obedience to God or fall behind in disobeying Him. Ibn ʿAbbās said: whoever wishes follows obedience to God, and whoever wishes falls behind it. Qatādah likewise said it means advancing in obedience to God or falling behind in disobedience to Him.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “Every soul is held in pledge for what it has earned, except the people of the right, who are in gardens asking about the guilty: ‘What brought you into Saqar?’ They will say, ‘We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor, and we used to indulge with those who indulged’” (74:38–45).

Every accountable soul is held in Hell for the disobedience it committed in this world, “except the people of the right,” who are not held in pledge, but are “in gardens asking about the guilty.” Ibn ʿAbbās said each person is held accountable for their deeds. Qatādah said everyone is confined except the people of the right. Mujāhid said they will not be brought to account. Ibn Zayd said the people of the right are not held for their sins; God forgives them. He recited
“except God’s purified servants”

explaining that God does not hold them to account for their evil deeds, but forgives and overlooks them as He promised. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said any soul for which punishment has been decreed is held by God in the Fire, but God does not hold anyone from the people of Paradise. He cited “Every soul is held in pledge… except the people of the right, who are in gardens asking…” Ibn ʿAbbās said if punishment had been decreed for someone, their place would be set in the Fire, where they would be held; no one from the people of Paradise is held.
They are in gardens asking one another.
The interpreters differed over who the people of the right are.
Some said they are Muslim children.
Among those who said this: ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, explained them as children. Another report from ʿAlī says they are Muslim children. Other reports from ʿAlī give the same explanation.
Others said they are angels. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are angels.

Those who said they are children or angels did so because these groups had no sins. They reasoned that they would not ask the guilty, “What brought you into Saqar?” unless they themselves had committed no sin in this world. If they had sinned and knew sin, they would not ask what caused the guilty to enter Saqar, because every child of Adam who enters Paradise after reaching the age of accountability and being bound by the commands and prohibitions knows that no one is punished except for disobedience. Regarding “who are in gardens asking about the guilty: ‘What brought you into Saqar?’”: the people of the right are in gardens, asking the guilty who were placed in Saqar, “What brought you into Saqar?”

Regarding “They will say, ‘We were not among those who prayed’”: the guilty will say to them that in this world they did not pray to God alone. “Nor did we feed the poor” means they were miserly with what God had granted them and withheld the poor person’s due. “We used to indulge with those who indulged” means we engaged in falsehood and what God dislikes along with everyone who did so. Qatādah said: whenever a misguided person went astray, they went astray with him. Another report from Qatādah says they used to say: whenever someone went astray, we went astray with him.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “We used to deny the Day of Judgment, until certainty came to us. The intercession of intercessors will not benefit them. What is the matter with them that they turn away from the Reminder?” (74:46–49).
Abū Jaʿfar, may God have mercy on him, said:

Regarding “We used to deny the Day of Judgment”: they will say, “We denied the Day of recompense, reward, and punishment; we did not believe in reward, punishment, or reckoning.” “Until certainty came to us” means until certain death came to us. “The intercession of intercessors will not benefit them” means the intercession of those God permits to intercede for sinful monotheists will not benefit them. This verse clearly shows that God allows some of His creation to intercede for others.

The interpreters said similarly. ʿAbd Allāh related a report about intercession: angels, prophets, martyrs, righteous people, and believers will intercede, and God will permit them to intercede. Then He will say, “I am the Most Merciful of the merciful,” and bring more people out of the Fire than all the people who had previously been brought out. Then He will say, “I am the Most Merciful of the merciful.” ʿAbd Allāh recited to the disbelievers: “What brought you into Saqar? They will say: We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor, and we used to indulge with those who indulged, and we used to deny the Day of Judgment.” He counted four on his hand, then said: “Do you see any good in these people? No one with any good will be left in it.” Abū al-Zarʿāʾ related that ʿAbd Allāh said: “Only four—or people with four [traits]—will remain in the Fire”; Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī was uncertain.

He then recited the verses listing the four reasons they entered Saqar. Qatādah said “The intercession of intercessors will not benefit them” teaches you that God will allow believers to intercede on the Day of Resurrection.

c: It was related to us that
m: the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: “Among my community is a man through whose intercession God will admit more people to Paradise than the tribe of Tamīm.” Al-Ḥasan said: “More than Rabīʿah and Muḍar.” We were told that a martyr intercedes for seventy members of his household. Qatādah said this teaches you that God permits some people to intercede for others. It is related that a man will intercede for two or three people. Abū Qilābah said God will admit to Paradise through the intercession of one man from this community as many people as the tribe of Tamīm—or more. Al-Ḥasan said, “As many as Rabīʿah and Muḍar.”

x: Regarding “What is the matter with them that they turn away from the Reminder?”: What is wrong with these polytheists that they turn away from God’s reminder to them in this Qur’an, not listening so that they may take heed and learn a lesson? Qatādah explained it as turning away from this Qur’an.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “As though they were frightened donkeys fleeing from a lion. Rather, each one of them wants to be given unrolled scriptures. No indeed! They do not fear the Hereafter” (74:50–53).

What is wrong with these polytheists that they turn away from the Reminder, turning away like frightened donkeys “fleeing from a lion”? The reciters differed over “mustanfirah.” Most Medinese reciters read it with fatḥah on the fāʾ, meaning frightened by the lion; most Kufan and Basran reciters, along with some Meccans, read it with kasrah, meaning fleeing. In our view both are established readings with sound meanings; whichever is recited is correct. Al-Farrāʾ said both fatḥah and kasrah are common in Arabic. He cited: “Hold your donkey, for it is fleeing after she-asses that have set out toward the west.” Regarding “fleeing from a lion,” the interpreters differed about the meaning of qaswarah.

Some said it means archers. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as archers. Abū Mūsā likewise said archers, as did Mujāhid. Other reports from Mujāhid give the same meaning. Mujāhid said it means a band of hunters, archers. Al-Ḥārith added that some said qaswarah means a lion and others said archers. ʿIkrimah said it means archers. A man asked him, “Doesn’t it mean lion in the Abyssinian language?” ʿIkrimah replied, “The Abyssinian word for lion is ʿanbasah.” Another report from ʿIkrimah says it means archers. Ibn ʿAbbās said they are archers. Qatādah said they are archers and hunters. Another report from Qatādah says qaswarah means arrows.
Others said it means hunters. Ibn ʿAbbās explained it as men who hunt. Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also said they are hunters; another report from him gives the same.

Others said it means groups of men. Ibn ʿAbbās said: “I do not know that any Arab uses the word for ‘lion’; it means bands of men.” Another report from him says it means a gathering of men, and he cited a pre-Islamic woman’s verse: “Daughter, be a good match for a good man; her maternal uncles among the tribe are the people of qaswarah.”
Others said it means the voices of men. Ibn ʿAbbās said qaswarah is the murmur of people—their voices. Sufyān cited
“Do you perceive any one of them or hear from them a faint sound?”

Others said it is a lion. Abū Hurayrah said it means a lion; another report from him gives the same. Ibn Sīlān related that Abū Hurayrah used to explain “fleeing from a lion” as a lion. Other reports from Abū Hurayrah give the same. Ibn ʿAbbās said that in Arabic it is a lion, in Persian shār, in Nabataean aryā, and in Abyssinian qaswarah. Ibn ʿAbbās also explained it as a lion. Ibn Zayd said qaswarah is a lion. Regarding “Rather, each one of them wants to be given unrolled scriptures”: Their turning away from this Qur’an is not because they do not know it is from God,

evidence.text: Most Medinese reciters read it with fatḥah on the fāʾ, meaning frightened by the lion; most Kufan and Basran reciters, along with some Meccans, read it with kasrah, meaning fleeing.
In our view both are established readings with sound meanings; whichever is recited is correct.

x: but each man among them wants a book to descend from heaven specifically to him.

The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said some people told Muḥammad: “If you want us to follow you, bring each of us a book addressed specifically to him and commanding us to follow you.” Qatādah said they wanted a certificate of innocence without doing any work. Mujāhid said each wanted scriptures sent down from the Lord of the worlds to a specific person. Regarding “No indeed! They do not fear the Hereafter”: Their claim that they would believe if they received unrolled scriptures is false. Rather, they do not fear God’s punishment and do not believe in resurrection, reward, or punishment,

and that is what led them to turn away from God’s reminder and made it easy for them to refuse to listen to His revelation. Qatādah said what corrupted them was that they did not believe in or fear the Hereafter. Qatādah said it was their failure to believe in and fear the Hereafter that corrupted them.

Interpretation of the words of God, mighty and exalted: “No indeed! It is a reminder; so whoever wishes may remember it. They will not remember unless God wills. He is worthy of being feared and worthy of granting forgiveness” (74:54–56).

“No indeed! It is a reminder” means the matter is not as these polytheists claim about this Qur’an—that it is transmitted magic and human speech. Rather, it is a reminder from God to His creation, by which He admonishes them.
The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah explained “No indeed! It is a reminder” as the Qur’an.

Regarding “so whoever wishes may remember it”: whoever among God’s servants, whom He has admonished through this Qur’an, wishes may remember it, take heed, and act according to its commands and prohibitions. “They will not remember unless God wills” means they will not remember this Qur’an, take heed from it, and act according to it unless God wills that they do so. No one can do anything unless God wills it and gives them the ability to do it.

Regarding “He is worthy of being feared and worthy of granting forgiveness”: God is worthy of having His servants fear His punishment for disobeying Him, avoid His prohibitions, and hasten to obey Him. “And worthy of granting forgiveness” means He is worthy of forgiving their sins if they do so and of not punishing them after they repent.

The interpreters said similarly. Qatādah said: “Our Lord deserves that His prohibitions be avoided, and He is worthy of forgiveness; He forgives sins.” Another report from Qatādah says: “He is worthy of having His prohibitions avoided, and worthy of forgiving sins.” This concludes the commentary on Sūrat al-Muddaththir.

notes.en: Al-Suyūṭī attributed it in al-Durr al-manthūr 6/286 to ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir.
notes.ar: عزاه السيوطي في الدر المنثور 6/ 286 إلى عبد بن حميد وابن المنذر.

notes.en: Reported by ʿAbd al-Razzāq in his Tafsīr 2/332 from Maʿmar.
notes.ar: أخرجه عبد الرزاق في تفسيره 2/ 332 عن معمر به.
